prompt_free_text:
This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features. The central claim is that although recent CBM constructions can match feature-based predictors on the source domain, they can fail badly under deployment-time distribution shift, and that this can be remedied by adapting both the concept bank and the concept-to-label predictor using only unlabeled target data and no source samples. The proposed method, CONDA, combines three stages: concept-score alignment (CSA), linear probing adaptation (LPA), and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concepts online. The paper also aims to provide a conceptual taxonomy of failure modes for CBMs under low-level and concept-level shifts.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and timely. The problem is important: interpretability methods are often evaluated only in-distribution, while deployment robustness is exactly where interpretable pipelines are supposed to matter most. The paper also addresses a relatively underexplored intersection of topics: concept bottlenecks, foundation models, and source-free/test-time adaptation. Empirically, the results suggest that adaptation can substantially improve target-domain performance for several CBM constructions, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift, where unadapted CBMs degrade sharply. The paper is also generally well motivated, and the decomposition into adapting concepts, adapting the classifier, and adding residual concepts is intuitive.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the technical framing, the strength of the empirical evidence relative to the claims, and some methodological choices that make it difficult to assess whether the gains come from “adaptive concept bottlenecks” per se or from fairly standard pseudo-label-based adaptation applied to a linear head over frozen FM features. My overall assessment is positive on novelty and practical relevance, but mixed on rigor.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation at a high level. The observation in Figure 1 and Table 1—that concept-based predictors are not automatically more robust than direct feature-based predictors—is valuable and worth documenting. This is a useful corrective to an overly optimistic narrative around CBMs. The proposed failure modes are also directionally sensible: concept extraction itself may be unstable under low-level perturbations; the concept-to-label mapping may fail under semantic/contextual shifts; and the concept set may simply be incomplete. This decomposition gives a plausible rationale for the three adaptation modules.

The empirical results are also promising in several places. On Waterbirds and Metashift, CONDA often recovers a large fraction of the gap between unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines, and sometimes nearly matches zero-shot performance. The gains are especially notable for worst-group accuracy, which is the right metric to emphasize for spurious-correlation benchmarks. The fact that the method is tested across multiple CBM construction approaches is another strength, since it suggests some degree of generality beyond a single concept-bank pipeline.

However, the paper’s formal treatment of distribution shift is not yet convincing. The definitions in Section 2.2 are mathematically dressed up, but they do not seem to support the later claims in a meaningful way. In particular, defining “low-level shift” as one that leaves the concept-score distribution unchanged and “concept-level shift” as one that changes concept scores but not prediction distributions is more a post hoc categorization than an operational characterization. Real corruptions and contextual shifts will not satisfy these equalities exactly, and the paper does not derive any theorem or guarantee from these definitions. As written, the formalism risks giving an impression of rigor without actually constraining the method or analysis. Definition 1 of concept completeness is also too weak to be useful: existence of some classifier mapping concepts to labels across domains is not something the method can test or exploit directly, and it conflates sufficiency with invariance. I would encourage the authors either to simplify this section and present it as an informal taxonomy, or to strengthen it with actual propositions linking the failure modes to the proposed objectives.

A related issue is that the CSA objective relies on source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics of concept scores, but the source-free setting is described as having no access to source data. The paper resolves this by assuming access to per-class means and covariances. This is reasonable in practice, but it is not cost-free: these statistics are a nontrivial summary of the source distribution, and for large concept spaces or many classes they may be substantial. More importantly, the method’s success may depend heavily on the quality of these stored statistics and on the Gaussian assumption. The paper does not really test this dependence. Since CSA is one of the main conceptual contributions, I would expect ablations on diagonal versus full covariance, sensitivity to covariance shrinkage, and perhaps comparisons to simpler alignment objectives that do not require class-conditional source summaries.

The pseudo-labeling strategy is another major source of concern. The method uses an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictions from the FM and chooses the more confident class. This is likely a strong signal, and in some datasets it may already be close to the final answer. In that case, adapting the CBM to mimic these pseudo-labels may simply distill a stronger non-interpretable predictor into the concept head. That is not necessarily a bad idea, but it weakens the claim that the method is specifically solving CBM robustness rather than transferring robustness from the FM baselines. This concern is especially salient because the paper repeatedly compares adapted CBMs to zero-shot and linear-probe baselines, yet those same baselines are used to generate supervision during adaptation. The comparison is therefore not clean. At minimum, the paper should report the pseudo-label accuracy itself, and ideally compare against a direct adaptation baseline that applies the same pseudo-labeling and optimization budget to a non-concept linear head over FM features. Without such a control, it is hard to isolate the value added by the concept bottleneck structure.

This issue also affects the interpretability claims. If the adapted CBM is trained to match pseudo-labels from a stronger black-box predictor, then the resulting concepts may be post hoc rationalizations of that predictor rather than independently meaningful causal abstractions. The qualitative Waterbirds examples are suggestive, but they are not enough to establish that the adapted concepts are more faithful, stable, or useful. In fact, one of the reported findings is that after adaptation, land-related concepts begin to positively contribute to predicting waterbirds because the target-domain correlations changed. This may be pragmatically useful, but it is not obviously an interpretability improvement in the usual CBM sense; it may instead reflect adaptation to a new spurious correlation. The paper should be more careful here. “Better aligned with the test data” is not the same as “more semantically faithful” or “more causally robust.” Stronger interpretability evaluation would help, such as concept intervention tests, concept completeness/sufficiency metrics, human evaluation of residual concept labels, or stability of top concepts across nearby inputs.

There are also several empirical inconsistencies that deserve more discussion. In Table 1, CONDA sometimes hurts performance, including fairly noticeably for the Yeh et al. CBM on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, and for some Camelyon17 settings. The paper acknowledges that different components matter under different shifts, but the main method is still presented as a unified three-stage pipeline. If CSA alone often outperforms the full method under low-level shifts, and LPA alone can match or exceed the full method under concept-level shifts, then the combined method may be over-adapting. This is important because online TTA methods are notoriously brittle. The paper should discuss when and why each stage hurts, and ideally provide a mechanism for selectively activating modules based on shift diagnostics. As it stands, the method seems somewhat heuristic.

The comparison set is also incomplete. Since the final predictor in Eq. (5) is still linear in the FM features, one natural baseline is simply source-free adaptation of a linear probe on FM features using the same pseudo-labels and online protocol. Another important baseline would be adapting the original CBM only through entropy minimization or standard TTA objectives, to show that the proposed CSA/RCB structure matters beyond generic adaptation. The paper cites TENT, CAFA, MEMO, etc., but does not appear to compare against them in the main results. Given the claim of being the first TTA method for CBMs, it is especially important to benchmark against straightforward adaptations of existing TTA methods to the CBM setting.

I also found the residual concept bottleneck somewhat under-justified. The idea of adding residual concepts is sensible and related to recent residual/incremental CBM work, but in this paper the residual concepts are initialized randomly and optimized only from pseudo-labels plus similarity/coherency regularization. It is not clear why these vectors should correspond to semantically meaningful concepts rather than arbitrary discriminative directions. The coherency term encourages high activation on top-k neighbors, but many non-semantic directions can satisfy that. The automated annotation procedure is relegated to the appendix, and the main text’s claim that residual concepts correspond to “feathers,” “wings,” and “beak” is intriguing but anecdotal. More systematic evidence is needed, especially because the residual branch is the component most directly tied to the paper’s “adaptive concept bank” narrative.

Another concern is fairness of the source-domain and target-domain comparisons. The paper uses different FM backbones across datasets, including a robustified CLIP variant for CIFAR and BioMedCLIP for Camelyon17. This is reasonable for performance, but it complicates the interpretation of robustness claims. In particular, if the pseudo-labels come from a robust FM and the CBM is adapted to imitate them, then the gains may depend strongly on backbone robustness. The paper briefly notes this, but I would like to see a clearer analysis of how much CONDA helps when the FM is weaker or less robust. Otherwise, the method may be best understood as a way to preserve FM robustness through an interpretable head, which is still useful, but narrower than the current framing suggests.

There are also some technical and presentation issues. The Mahalanobis distance formula in Section 3.1 appears to have a parenthesis typo. Equation numbering is inconsistent in a few places, and there are many grammatical errors and typos throughout the manuscript. More importantly, some claims are overstated. For example, the abstract says the method “aligns the CBM performance with that of non-interpretable classification,” but Table 1 shows this is not uniformly true. On Waterbirds, adapted CBMs remain well below the source LP baseline and only roughly match zero-shot. On Camelyon17 and CIFAR100, the picture is mixed depending on the CBM construction. The claims should be softened to reflect that the method often narrows the gap, sometimes substantially, but does not consistently eliminate it.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, add stronger baselines: a pseudo-label-adapted linear probe over FM features, generic TTA objectives applied to the CBM head, and perhaps an ablation where pseudo-labels come only from the unadapted CBM rather than FM baselines. Second, report pseudo-label accuracy and calibration, since the method depends critically on them. Third, strengthen the interpretability evaluation beyond qualitative examples, ideally with intervention-based or faithfulness-oriented metrics. Fourth, clarify the role and cost of stored source statistics in the source-free setting, and test CSA sensitivity to the Gaussian assumption. Fifth, analyze failure cases and negative transfer more carefully, especially when the full three-stage method underperforms simpler subsets. Sixth, either simplify the formal shift taxonomy or turn it into something more substantive with theoretical or empirical validation.

In terms of significance, I think the paper opens an interesting direction. If one wants interpretable deployment-time adaptation on top of frozen foundation models, this is a natural and important problem. The proposed modular approach is plausible and the empirical gains are nontrivial. But in its current form, the paper does not yet fully disentangle what is specifically new about adaptive concept bottlenecks from what is inherited from strong FM pseudo-labels and standard online adaptation. The interpretability claims are also suggestive rather than firmly established.

My recommendation would be borderline positive if the venue values novelty and emerging directions, but with clear reservations about rigor and evaluation. I would encourage acceptance only if the authors can better position the contribution as an empirical/methodological first step and temper the stronger claims. As a final summary: the paper addresses an important problem and presents promising results, but it needs stronger controls, cleaner causal attribution of gains, and more rigorous interpretability validation to fully support its conclusions.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It argues that although FM-based CBMs can be accurate and interpretable on the source domain, they often degrade substantially under low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts. The proposed method, CONDA, adapts a deployed CBM using only unlabeled target data and no source samples through three stages: (1) Concept Score Alignment (CSA), which updates concept vectors to align target concept-score distributions to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics using pseudo-labels and Mahalanobis distances; (2) Linear Probing Adaptation (LPA), which updates the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-label cross-entropy with elastic-net regularization; and (3) Residual Concept Bottleneck (RCB), which adds new residual concepts and a residual linear head to compensate for incomplete concept sets. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to or above zero-shot / linear-probe FM baselines. The paper also presents qualitative evidence that adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: adapting interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines at test time under distribution shift, rather than only adapting black-box classifiers.
The proposed framework is modular and intuitively matched to distinct failure modes: concept misalignment, classifier mismatch, and concept incompleteness.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple FM backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods, which strengthens the practical relevance of the study.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs on several benchmarks, especially under concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.
The paper includes component-wise analysis suggesting different stages matter for different shift types, which helps justify the design.
The qualitative interpretability analysis is a useful addition and aligns with the paper's motivation of preserving or improving concept-based explanations after adaptation.
weaknesses: The paper's formalization of shift types is overly restrictive and partly disconnected from the actual adaptation setting; in particular, defining low-level shift by exact equality of concept-score distributions is unrealistic and makes the subsequent failure-mode discussion somewhat tautological.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-labels from zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictors, so much of the adaptation signal comes from non-interpretable models rather than the CBM itself; this weakens the claim that the method robustly adapts the interpretable pipeline in a self-contained way.

The comparison set is limited: there is no strong baseline that directly adapts the equivalent linear classifier in feature space under the same pseudo-labeling and online TTA protocol, making it hard to isolate the benefit of concept-specific adaptation versus generic adaptation.

Some reported results indicate adaptation can hurt performance substantially (e.g., several CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 settings, and zero-shot adaptation on Waterbirds/Metashift), but the paper does not sufficiently characterize when or why CONDA fails.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative and anecdotal; there is no rigorous quantitative metric showing that adapted or residual concepts are more faithful, stable, or human-meaningful.
The method introduces several stages and hyperparameters, but the main text gives limited evidence on sensitivity, robustness, or computational overhead in realistic deployment settings.
methodological_flaws: There is a scientific-logic inconsistency in Section 2.2/2.3: low-level shift is defined as one that does not change the concept-score distribution, yet failure mode 1 is 'non-robust concept bottleneck under low-level shift' where the concept-score distribution does change. This means the failure mode contradicts the earlier definition rather than analyzing a shift category under the same assumptions. The taxonomy is therefore not logically clean.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it is phrased in terms of equality of prediction distributions across domains, not correctness with respect to labels. A classifier could satisfy the definition while being wrong on both domains, so the notion does not capture sufficiency of concepts for accurate prediction.

The CSA objective assumes class-conditional Gaussian distributions of source concept scores and access to their means/covariances, but there is no empirical validation that this approximation is adequate, especially for high-dimensional concept spaces or heterogeneous CBM constructions. If covariances are poorly estimated or singular, Mahalanobis-based adaptation may be unstable.

The pseudo-labeling protocol may leak substantial target-task supervision from stronger FM predictors into the CBM adaptation. Since the adapted CBM is trained to mimic pseudo-labels from zero-shot/linear-probe models, gains may largely reflect distillation from those models rather than principled domain adaptation of concepts. This threatens the causal interpretation of the reported improvements.

The empirical evaluation does not cleanly test the claimed contribution of concept adaptation against simpler alternatives. Because Eq. (5) is effectively a linear classifier over FM features factorized into concept matrices and weights, a direct feature-space residual linear adaptation baseline with the same pseudo-labels would be a necessary control. Without it, it is unclear whether the concept bottleneck structure itself is responsible for the gains.

The residual branch weakens interpretability guarantees: randomly initialized residual concepts are optimized primarily for pseudo-label cross-entropy, with only weak similarity/coherency regularization. There is no proof or strong empirical evidence that these residual vectors correspond to semantically meaningful concepts rather than arbitrary discriminative directions.

Some equations and notation appear error-prone or inconsistent. For example, the Mahalanobis distance expression in Section 3.1 is malformed in the text, Eq. (5) is later referred to as Eq. (3) in places, and the coherence objective sign convention in Eq. (14) is easy to misread. These issues do not invalidate the idea but reduce confidence in mathematical precision.

The evaluation emphasizes AVG and WG improvements but does not report calibration, pseudo-label accuracy, or adaptation stability across batch orderings, despite using online sequential adaptation. Since online TTA can be highly order-sensitive, omission of such analyses leaves empirical validity incomplete.
